title: How to Date With Wisdom
excerpt: Most dating advice is either too casual or too anxious. There is a third way, slower than the culture and warmer than the rulebook.
body:
I have watched two kinds of Christian dating fail, and they fail in opposite directions. One treats it like shopping, swiping through people the way you scroll a menu, always wondering if a better option is one screen away. The other treats it like defusing a bomb, so heavy with rules and red flags and spiritual interrogation that no actual human can survive the first three coffees. Both miss the point. Dating is not a marketplace and it is not a doctrinal exam. It is how you find out, honestly and over time, whether you and another person could build a life that serves God together.

## Date toward marriage, not toward feelings

The culture dates toward feelings. You go out to see if the spark is there, and when it fades, as feeling always does, you assume the relationship is over. This produces a string of intense beginnings and no endings that mean anything.

Wisdom dates toward a question, not a feeling. The question is simple: could I become more like Christ alongside this person, and could they become more like Christ alongside me? Attraction matters and I am not pretending it does not. But attraction is the doorway, not the house. Plenty of people you are attracted to would make your faith smaller. Date toward who you would become, not toward how you feel in the first month.

## Watch character before chemistry

Chemistry tells you almost nothing about whether someone will be faithful when faithfulness is expensive. Character tells you everything. So watch the things chemistry distracts you from. How do they treat the server, the waiter, the person who can do nothing for them? What do they do when they are wrong? Do they apologize cleanly, or do they manage you into thinking it was your fault?

The Bible's word for the thing you are looking for is steadfastness, the quality of someone who keeps their word when keeping it costs them. You cannot see it in a good week. You see it in how they handle disappointment, traffic, their family, and being told no. Slow down enough to see those things before you decide.

## Bring it into the light

Dating in secret is dating in danger. The relationships that go badly wrong, morally and otherwise, are almost always the ones nobody else can see. So let people see it. Introduce them to your friends early, not because you are sure, but because you want people who love you watching while your judgment is compromised by hope.

Ask a married couple you trust to know the person. Ask them to tell you the truth, even the truth you do not want. Proverbs says there is safety in many counselors (Proverbs 11:14), and it does not add an exception for romance. Your friends can see what you cannot, because they are not falling for anyone.

## Guard the body and the timeline

I am not going to give you a rulebook for physical boundaries, because rulebooks get gamed and the point is not the rule. The point is that physical intimacy bonds two people faster than knowledge can keep up, and a body convinced it is married will lie to a mind that is still deciding. Go slower than your body wants. The slowness is not prudishness. It is keeping your judgment unbribed.

And watch the timeline. Endless dating with no movement toward decision is its own kind of dishonesty, a way of taking the comfort of a relationship without the risk of committing to one. If after a reasonable time you cannot say yes, it is more loving to say no than to keep someone in a holding pattern your indecision built.

## This week

Name one thing about the person you are dating, or the kind of person you want to date, that has nothing to do with how they make you feel. Watch for it this week. If you are not dating anyone, ask one married couple you respect what they actually look for in a spouse. Their answer will teach you more than any list.

Dating with wisdom is slower than the culture and warmer than the rulebook. It is not about finding a flawless person. It is about telling the truth, in the light, with people watching, toward a life you could build together.
